en: *An Explanation of the Buddha’s Forty-two Chapter Sutra*, composed by the Ming-dynasty exegete Zhixu of Ou-yi, Ancient Wu.
Regarding the seven characters of the sutra title: they present both the general and the specific, manifesting both the person and the Dharma. The character "Sutra" (*jing*) is the general name.
All the Sūtra-piṭakas of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are collectively termed "Sūtras.

The six characters of the "Forty-two Sections" spoken by the Buddha constitute its specific name, as it differs from other sūtras. Within this specific name, the Buddha is the person who is the speaker.
The Forty-two Sections constitute the Dharma that was taught. Regarding the term "Buddha": in the Sanskrit language it is fully called *Buddha*, which is translated here as "the Awakened One.
This means one who is self-awakened, awakened others, and whose practice of awakening is perfected. Being self-awakened distinguishes him from ordinary beings;
being awakened others distinguishes him from those of the Two Vehicles; and the perfection of awakening distinguishes him from Bodhisattvas. He is thus Śākyamuni Tathāgata, the myriad...
The Venerable One of Virtue and Compassion is the Teacher of the Sahā world. To "expound" means to express what is cherished in one's heart. The Buddha cherishes the salvation of sentient beings;

when the conditions and opportunities have not yet matured, he remains silent, awaiting the proper time. Once the conditions and opportunities have ripened, he administers medicine according to the ailment.
The "Forty-two Sections" is a title designated by way of its numerical count; it is drawn from among the teachings given throughout his entire lifetime.
I have extracted the most essential and concise portions and compiled them into a single volume to suit the spiritual capacities of those in this land.
Thus, while the text is brief, the meaning is vast; it encompasses all four teachings and should not be hastily categorized as merely Hinayana.
Translated later during the Later Han by Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna.
"Later Han" refers to the Eastern Han; it is so called in contrast to the Former Han. This was in the third year of the Yongping era of Emperor Xiaoming.
In the year of Gengshen, the Emperor dreamed of a golden man with a halo of light around his neck flying into the palace courtyard.
He questioned his ministers about it, and the Grand Astrologer Fu Yi replied, "Your servant has heard that there is a deity in the Western Regions called Buddha;

the one Your Majesty dreamed of must surely be him. The Court Doctor Wang Zun also submitted a memorial, stating: "According to the *Zhou Shu Yiji* (Records of Marvels from the Book of Zhou), it records—"
The Buddha was born in the twenty-sixth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty, the year of Jiayin. At that time, the rivers overflowed and the great earth shook;
a light of five colors pierced through the Taiwei constellation. The Grand Astrologer Suyou performed a divination and obtained the fifth line of the Qian hexagram.
"A dragon soars in the heavens. This refers to the Great Sage of the Western Regions. A thousand years hence, his teachings and influence shall spread to this land.
The King commanded that an inscription be carved in stone and buried at the Southern Suburb. Later, during the time of King Mu of Zhou, heaven and earth shook;
twelve white rainbows pierced the sun and traversed the sky. The Grand Astrologer Hu Duo divined these omens.
This was said to be an omen of the Great Sage of the West entering nirvana.

In the seventh year, under the cyclical sign of Jiazi, Emperor Ming issued an edict to the Langzhong Cai Yin, the Zhonglangjiang Qin Jing, the Bolishi Wang Zun, and seventeen others—eighteen people in total—to travel westward in search of the Buddha-dharma.
Upon reaching the kingdom of India, they invited Kāśyapa Mātanga and Zhu Falan.
Using a white horse to carry the scriptures, as well as the śarīra relics and painted Buddha images, he arrived at Luoyang in the tenth year of Yongping, the year of Dingmao.
The Emperor was delighted and established the Baima Monastery. There, the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* was translated.
On the first day of the first month of the fourteenth year, the Daoist masters of the Five Peaks, including Chu Shanxin, harbored resentment and were displeased.
He submitted a memorial requesting a formal contest. Thereupon, on the fifteenth day, a great assembly gathered at the southern gate of Baima Temple.

Kāśyapa Mātanga and his colleagues placed the various scriptures of the *Lingbao* upon an altar to the east of the road. The Emperor placed the scriptures, images, and śarīra relics upon a pavilion of seven treasures to the west of the road.
Kāśyapa Mātanga and his colleagues circumambulated the altar while weeping; they invoked the Celestial Honored One with words of such profound sincerity that—
When the sandalwood fuel and other materials were burned according to the scriptures, it was hoped that the sutra would remain undamaged; however, they were all reduced to ashes.
The various arts previously employed—such as ascending to heaven, entering fire, walking upon water, and concealing one's form—all ceased to be effective.
Yet the Buddha’s relics emitted light of five colors that rose straight into the air, circling like a canopy to cover the entire assembly and eclipsing the sun. At this, Kāśyapa Mātanga...
Through the supernormal power of the divine feet (*ṛddhipāda*), he flew, sat, and lay down in mid-air, manifesting transformations with sovereign ease.
Heavenly rain fell of precious flowers, and various musical instruments were played; the assembly was filled with joy at such an unprecedented occurrence.
This was the beginning of the Buddha-dharma’s entry into Zhendan (China). According to records, Kāśyapa Mātanga and Zhu Falan were both natives of Central India; these are their two names.

In neither case is there a reversal [of the original meaning]. What is called "translation" (yi) refers to replacing those Indic words with Chinese words so that the people of this land may understand their meaning.

After the World-Honored One had attained enlightenment, he reflected: "Detachment from desire and tranquility are supreme. Abiding in great meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), he subdued all demonic paths.
In the Deer Park, he turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths, delivering the five men including Kauṇḍinya so that they realized the fruits of the Path.
Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who spoke of various doubts and sought the Buddha’s guidance; thus it was with the World-Honored One.
The instructions were given one by one, bringing about full awakening; with palms joined in respectful assent, they complied with the Honored One’s commands.
The general prefaces of all sutras contain six elements of verified faith: first, the essence of the Dharma; second, the hearer; third, the responsive stimulus of the capacity for awakening.
There are four [factors]: the teacher, five [factors]: the location, and six [factors]: those who heard together—namely, "Thus have I heard:
at one time the Buddha was in such-and-such a place," and so forth. The sequence in the present text differs slightly from the general convention;

this is because when the Buddha-dharma first arrived, it followed the stylistic conventions of the local script, which values brevity. Nevertheless, upon careful examination, all six meanings are fully contained therein.
The two characters "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān) indicate the Teacher. The three characters "having attained enlightenment" indicate the responsive capacity of the disciples.
"In the Deer Park" indicates the location. "Kauṇḍinya and others, as well as other bhikṣus" indicates those who hear the teaching and the other listeners.
"The turning of the wheel of Dharma" indicates the essence of the Dharma. According to this single passage, it is further divided into four [sections].
Section. First, from "After the World-Honored One had attained enlightenment" (one sentence), there is a general account of the origins of his entire ministry.
Second, from "Then he thought thus" up to "subduing the various māras," there is a retrospective account of the method by which he attained enlightenment.

Third, from "In the Deer Park" up to "realizing the fruit of the Way" (three sentences), there is a specific account of the beginning of the turning of the Dharma wheel. Fourth, from "Furthermore... [the text continues].
The Bhikṣu, having respectfully obeyed the venerable command, then proceeded to formally narrate the origin of this sutra. Regarding the first passage, "The World-Honored One":

this refers to our Śākyamuni Tathāgata, the God among gods and the Sage among sages, who alone is called "Venerable" within the entire vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), and the world of all perfectly awakened ones (*buddha-loka*).

Furthermore, regarding the one who attained enlightenment: if one were to discuss the actual time since the World-Honored One truly realized the Buddha-way, it has already been an incalculable number of kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, as clarified in the "Life Span" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

Now, for the sake of sentient beings with whom he shares a karmic affinity in this land, he manifested his dwelling at the assembly of Kāśyapa Buddha during the past age when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years.
During his stage as the Regent, he was reborn in the Inner Court of Tuṣita Heaven, where, with his pure divine eye, he observed those beings capable of being transformed.
Only when the life span of humans reached one hundred years did the conditions for transformation ripen; thereupon, he manifested the descent of his spirit into Kapilavastu in Central India.
His father’s name was Śuddhodana and his mother’s name was Māyā. He remained in the womb for ten months and was born from the left side of his mother.
Pointing one finger toward heaven and one finger toward the earth, he gazed in the four directions and took seven strides around.

He declared, "In all that is above heaven and below heaven, I alone am the most honored. Thereafter, he again manifested as a youth, learning all the various arts and excelling in every field beyond his peers.
When he reached the age of twenty-nine, he traveled through the four gates of the city and beheld an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and a śramaṇa.
Having resolved his mind upon leaving the household life, he scaled the city walls at the hour of midnight. With a golden blade, he shaved his hair and cast away all his precious ornaments.
Donning the hempen garments offered by a tree deity, he traveled to various kingdoms to study. First, he studied under Ārāḍa Kālāma, practicing the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness;
before long, he attained realization of it, but knowing it was not the ultimate goal, he abandoned it and departed. Next, he went to Udraka Rāmaputra...

The son practiced the meditative concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; he also attained realization before long, but knowing it was not ultimate, he abandoned it and departed.

Seeing various non-Buddhist practitioners competing to cultivate asceticism in their hope of attaining the Way, each taking three years as their limit but ultimately failing to achieve their goal, he sought to deliver them and thus went to the Snowy Mountains to demonstrate the practice of six years of austerity.
He practiced asceticism, consuming only one grain of hemp and one grain of wheat each day until his skin and bones clung together; yet he did not achieve the Way.

He then abandoned these austerities and accepted the offering of sixteen-fold refined milk-rice from a cowherd girl. His vital energy being fully restored, he proceeded to the river Nairañjanā, bathed his body, and emerged.
There he received the auspicious [alms-bowl] offered by Śakra, the Lord of Devas, who had manifested as a young boy.
He went to the Bodhi tree at Vajrāsana in the kingdom of Magadha, spread grass, and sat down cross-legged.
With the samādhi of loving-kindness, he subdued the armies of Māra; he entered deeply into the four dhyānas and contemplated the Four Noble Truths.
On the eighth night of the first month of winter, when the morning star appeared, he attained sudden and great enlightenment, realizing the path free from outflows. This is what constitutes a Buddha.
This was when the Jewel first appeared in the world. Regarding the subsequent passage, "He then reflected in this way," etc., this is a retrospective account of the time he sat beneath the tree.
By means of untaught wisdom and spontaneous wisdom, he realized that detachment from desire and tranquility are supreme;
therefore, he first rebuked and abandoned the evil and unwholesome dharmas of the desire realm, entered the first dhyāna accompanied by vitarka and vicāra, and subsequently again detached [from it].

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he entered the second dhyāna with internal clarity and mental unification. Next, by being detached from joy, he realized sublime bliss and entered the third dhyāna.
Then, having abandoned both suffering and pleasure, with equanimity and mindfulness purified, he entered the fourth dhyāna.

From within the fourth dhyāna, he suddenly gave rise to the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*), thereby tearing through the net of craving of Māra and severing the bonds of the views of the non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, the initial sentence regarding the attainment of the Way is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), by which one personally realizes *bodhi*.

The subsequent reflection and so forth constitute subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), whereby one again contemplates the Four Noble Truths as the basis for preaching the Dharma; this is the most supreme state of tranquility.

One then contemplates the Truth of Cessation and abides in the Great Dhyāna-concentration. One then contemplates the Truth of the Path. All Māras and non-Buddhists are subsumed within the two truths of Suffering and its Origin.
Regarding the Deer Park mentioned in the third section—also known as the Deer Garden—it is located in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī;
it is the place where the Buddha first turned the Wheel of Dharma. Turning the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths refers to Suffering, Origin, Cessation, and the Path.

These are called the Four Noble Truths. Suffering (*duḥkha*) is the fruit of the world; it refers specifically to the five aggregates (*skandhas*) of form and mind within the three realms and six destinies.

Origination (*samudaya*) is the cause of the world; it refers specifically to the afflictions (*kleśa*) of views and thoughts, as well as to out-flowing (*āsrava*) wholesome, unwholesome, and imperturbable karma.
Cessation (*nirodha*) is the fruit of the supramundane; it means that because the cause ceases, the fruit ceases, whereby one attains tranquility and the absence of [suffering].

For the sake of peace and happiness, the Path is the cause for transcending the world. Briefly stated, it consists of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*); extensively, it consists of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*). These are:

the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).
These four are all called "truths" (*satya*) because they are examined and verified as being real and not false. They are further named...

Regarding the Four Noble Truths: because they are realized and known only through noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), the Buddha, having personally realized and perceived the principle of these four truths, causes all sentient beings to hear and know them.
From within the Buddha’s subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), the sound of the Dharma flows forth and enters the hearts of sentient beings;
therefore, it is called a "wheel" (*cakra*). Furthermore, "wheel" carries the meaning of crushing and grinding.
By means of this teaching, it turns to destroy the various delusions of views and afflictions (*kleśa*) within sentient beings;

therefore, it is called a "wheel. There are three turnings of this Wheel of the Four Noble Truths. The first is the turning of demonstration: namely, "This is suffering," characterized by its nature of oppression;

"This is the origin," characterized by its nature of inciting [rebirth]; "This is cessation," characterized by its nature of being realizable; and "This is the path," characterized by its nature of being cultivable. The second...
The exhortation to turn [the wheel] means: "This is suffering; you should know it. This is its origin; you should abandon it.
This is its cessation; you should realize it. This is the path; you should cultivate it. The third is the turning through realization, which means: "This is suffering; I have already known it."
"This is the origin; it has been abandoned by me. This is cessation; it has been realized by me. This is the path; it has been cultivated by me.
Thus was the Jewel of the Dharma first manifested in the world. As for the five men, including Kauṇḍinya, they were: first, Aśvajit; [the others being Bhadrika, Vāṣpa, Mahānāman, and Aśvakin].
1. Aśvajit (translated as "Horse-Winner"). 2. Bāṣpa (translated as "Little Wise One"). 3. Kauṇḍinya, also named Mahānāman;
these three were all paternal kinsmen of the Buddha. 4. Ājñātakauṇḍinya (translated as "Fire-Vessel"). 5. Aśvakīrṇa, also named Bhāradvāja;
these two were both maternal uncles of the Buddha. When the Prince first left the city to renounce the world...
The King, his father, could not cease thinking of him and commanded these five men to search for him.
Since the Prince had vowed that he would not return, the five men did not dare go back to the kingdom; they thus remained in attendance upon him.

Once the Prince began practicing austerities, two of them, unable to endure such hardship, first fled away. Later, when the Prince accepted fine food, three of them took pleasure in the practice of austerity.
They, too, departed and each practiced a different path within the Deer Park. Once the Buddha had attained enlightenment, he perceived that these five men should be the first to receive liberation;
he therefore went to them. When he first turned the Wheel of Dharma, Ājñātakauṇḍinya was the first to awaken.
Subsequently, he taught the methods for practicing generosity, observing precepts, and being reborn in the heavens; he censured sensual desires as impure and praised renunciation as true happiness.
Aśvajit attained awakening immediately; at the third discourse on the Dharma, Kāśyapa and Kauṇḍinya also attained awakening.
This was the first appearance of the Saṅgha-ratna in the world. Regarding the phrase "furthermore, there were bhikṣus, etc. in the fourth section:
after the Buddha had already delivered these five bhikṣus, he subsequently delivered Yaśas and the other fifty-five people, as well as the three Kāśyapas and others.
One thousand people, including Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and two hundred others, followed this.
From that time forward, they delivered immeasurable numbers of people, causing them all to attain the nature of a bhikṣu. As for the term "bhikṣu," it is translated here as "remover of hunger.

This means that by fully upholding the two hundred and fifty pure precepts, one is fit to serve as a field of merit for the world of humans, thereby removing the [suffering] of sentient beings within the causal state.

This refers to the famine occurring at the time of the fruition [of karma]. Furthermore, it contains three meanings: first, the destruction of evil; second, the mendicant (bhikṣu); and third, the terrifying of Māra.
When it says that various doubts are resolved by seeking the Buddha’s guidance, it means determining what is permissible and what is not.
Joining the palms signifies listening to the Dharma with a single-minded focus, without indolence or distraction. The above constitutes the introduction; all that follows is the formal exposition.
The Buddha said: "One who leaves home to renounce kin, recognizes the mind and realizes the fundamental source, and understands the dharma of non-action, is called a śramaṇa.
Constantly practicing the two hundred and fifty precepts with pure conduct in every movement, they cultivate the four true paths of practice to become an arhat.
An arhat is one who can fly through the air and manifest transformations, possess a lifespan spanning vast kalpas, and cause the earth to tremble at will. Next is the stage of anāgāmin."
The Anāgāmin (Non-returner), at the end of his life, ascends to the nineteenth heaven and realizes Arhatship.
Next is the Sakṛdāgāmin (Once-returner). The Sakṛdāgāmin goes up once and returns once, then immediately attains Arhatship. Next is the Srotāpanna (Stream-enterer).
The Srotāpanna undergoes seven deaths and seven births, and then realizes Arhatship. One whose craving and desire are severed is like one whose four limbs have been cut off.
They are no longer employed.
This is the first chapter, which generally elucidates the distinctions among the realizations of the fruits of śrāmaṇya.

To realize the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, one must renounce one’s kin and leave the household life, recognize the mind and penetrate the fundamental source, and understand the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). For parents cannot...
If one grants this, then according to the Buddha-dharma, one is not permitted to leave the household life.

If one leaves the household life yet does not recognize the mind or penetrate the fundamental source, then although the body has departed from the secular world, one remains bound by conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and cannot be called a *śramaṇa*.

To "recognize the mind" means to understand that there are no phenomena apart from the mind, thereby awakening to the fact that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is fundamentally empty. To "penetrate the fundamental source" means to understand that the nature of the mind is without substantial reality. Thus...
Realizing that the dependent nature is like an illusion and understanding unconditioned phenomena means knowing that *tathatā* (suchness) and all phenomena are neither identical nor different;
this is the realization of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). The Sanskrit term *śramaṇa* is translated here as "diligent cessation.

This refers to diligently cultivating ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), while ceasing and extinguishing greed, hatred, and delusion. Constantly practicing the two hundred and fifty precepts is [the path of] increase.

The higher training in ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*) consists of pure conduct in both movement and stillness; the higher training in concentration (*adhicitta-śikṣā*) consists of the fourfold practice of the true path;

and the higher training in wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*) refers to cultivating the path by contemplating the Four Noble Truths. An *arhat* possesses three meanings: first, "slayer of the thieves" (*vadhaka*);
second, "worthy of offerings" (*dakṣiṇīya*); and third, "one who does not arise again" (*anutpāda*). This is the fourth stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) realized by the śramaṇa.

This is the fruit [of practice]: having completely severed the two delusions of views and thought within the three realms, one possesses the power of flight and transformation; this briefly illustrates one aspect of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
Regarding the lifespan of vast eons, it refers to the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomayakāya*), which are capable of abiding for a long time according to one's vows.
"Abiding and moving heaven and earth" refers to the place where Arhats dwell; there, both celestial deities and terrestrial spirits are all moved with awe.
Alternatively, it may mean that every single act or every single dwelling can shake heaven and earth. Anāgāmin—translated here as "Non-returner"—is the third fruit of the path.
Regarding the "nineteen heavens," these range from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of No Affliction (*Avṛha*). This constitutes the first...

20. Having transcended the nineteen lower heavens, because they have already severed the nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they realize arhatship within the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) and no longer return to the desire realm.
*Sakṛdāgāmin*—translated here as "Once-returner"—is the second fruit. They have already severed six grades of the afflictions of the desire realm; the remainder...
Three grades remain. Therefore, one [of these] goes to a heaven above the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while one returns to the human world and immediately realizes *arhatship*.

The *srotāpanna*—translated here as "Stream-enterer"—is the first fruit (*phala*). Having already severed the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) within the three realms, they have for the first time entered the stream of the noble ones (*ārya-srotas*) and will no longer fall into the three evil destinies.
However, because the nine grades of afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) in the desire realm remain entirely intact, they are able to...
They moisten seven births. This means that the spontaneous greed, hatred, delusion, and pride of the highest-superior grade (adhimātra-adhimātra) in the desire realm can moisten two births;

afflictions of the highest-middle grade (adhimātra-madhya) can moisten one birth; afflictions of the highest-lowest grade (adhimātra-mṛdu) also moisten one birth; afflictions of the middle-superior grade (madhya-adhimātra) also moisten one birth;
afflictions of the middle-middle grade (madhya-madhya) and middle-lowest grade (madhya-mṛdu) together moisten one birth; and [afflictions of] the lowest-superior grade (mṛdu-adhimātra)...
The afflictions of the lower-middle and lower-lower grades together moisten a single lifetime; only after seven cycles of birth and death does one realize the fruit of Arhatship.
This refers to those who abandon [afflictions] spontaneously (*anābhoga*). If they are abandoned through applied effort (*prayoga*), then it is not fixed.

Nevertheless, although the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) of the three realms comprise many grades and types, they are all fundamentally rooted in craving and desire (*tṛṣṇā*); once craving and desire are [eliminated], [the others follow].
Once severed, one emerges from the wheel of suffering; thus, it is likened to a limb: once severed, it can never again be used. The Buddha said:

"Those who have left the home life as śramaṇas sever desire and eliminate attachment. They recognize the source of their own minds, penetrate the profound principle of the Buddhas, and awaken to the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Internally they have nothing to acquire, and externally they have nothing to seek. Their minds are not bound to the Path, nor do they accumulate karma. No [karma].
Contemplate non-action: it is neither cultivated nor realized; without passing through the various stages, it is spontaneously supreme. This is called the Way.
This second chapter clarifies the realization of the fruits of the śramaṇa. Although there are distinctions [in the fruits], the principle realized is without distinction.
One severs the desire-love shared by ordinary beings and sages, recognizes the source of one’s own mind, and realizes that the self-clinging is fundamentally empty. Attaining...

The Buddha’s profound principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*): awakening to the unconditioned dharma of *tathatā* manifested by the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), severing the desire and attachment of the stage of residual conditioning through skillful means, and realizing that the source of one's own mind is such that the clinging to dharmas (*dharma-abhiniveśa*) is fundamentally empty. The Buddha’s profound principle of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*):

awakening to the unconditioned dharma of *tathatā* manifested by the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), severing the desire and attachment of the stage of true retribution and non-obstruction, and realizing...

The source of one's own mind is simultaneously empty and non-arising; one penetrates the profound principle of the Middle Truth of the Buddha and awakens to the unconditioned dharma of True Suchness (tathatā) manifested by that simultaneous emptiness.
Furthermore, one realizes that the desire and attachment of the three lands are themselves empty; this is called severing desire and removing attachment.

One realizes the source of one's own mind and understands that pervasive conceptualization is fundamentally empty. One penetrates the profound principle of the Buddha’s true reality: when all is empty, everything is empty;

there is nothing provisional and nothing intermediate that is not empty. Thus, one awakens to the meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha as "emptiness according to reality," which is termed the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
To fully understand that the desire and attachment of the three lands are merely provisional is called "cutting off desire and removing attachment.

To recognize the source of one's own mind as dependent and illusory, and to penetrate the profound principle of the Buddha’s conventional truth—that all is provisional, and there is nothing empty or middle that is not provisional—and to awaken to the meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha as truly non-empty, is called the "unconditioned dharma" (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). To fully understand the desire of the three lands...
Attachment is itself the Middle Way. To sever desire and eliminate attachment is to realize the source of one’s own mind as perfectly complete and inherently endowed.
One thereby penetrates the profound principle of the Buddha’s Middle Truth: that within the One, all things are the Middle; there is nothing empty or provisional that is not the Middle.

To awaken to the Tathāgatagarbha—transcending both identity and difference, being neither identical nor non-identical—is the meaning of the Unconditioned Dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). This Unconditioned Dharma is, from the very beginning, [self-existent...]

It exists. Because it does not belong to that which is newly produced, there is nothing to be attained within; there is only the single true mind. Because there is no phenomenon outside the mind, there is nothing to be sought without.
Knowing that phenomena are like a raft, the mind is not bound to the Path. Having severed the seeds of delusion, one also does not form karma.
Because one realizes the fundamental, non-discriminative, true wisdom, there is no thought. One realizes the inconceivable.

Subsequently, one attains provisional wisdom; thus, there is no "action. This is cultivation that accords with the nature (*dharmatā*); since cultivation is itself non-cultivation, it is not cultivation. One fully realizes the nature through realization;
since realization is itself non-realization, it is not realization. The various stages are like measuring the void with a ruler—the void is fundamentally not the ruler.
Furthermore, it is like entering the ocean: though one may distinguish its depths, those depths are nothing other than [the ocean itself].
It is like the great ocean; therefore, it is said that without passing through the various stages, one spontaneously honors the supreme, which is called the Way (*mārga*).

In the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) teaching, one realizes the truth through the cessation of causes; yet cessation is not itself the ultimate truth, so the ultimate truth does not pass through the various stages.

In the *Pratyekabuddha* (Shared) teaching, phenomena are entirely the truth; thus, the ultimate truth does not pass through the various stages. In the *Vaipulya* (Distinct) teaching, the Middle Way follows conditions without changing.
Therefore, the Middle Way does not pass through the various stages. In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), even a single color or a single fragrance is none other than the Middle Way;
thus, the Middle Way does not pass through the various stages. By means of the preceding chapter, one now understands that nature does not preclude cultivation;

by means of this present chapter, one understands that cultivation does not obstruct nature. By means of the preceding chapter, one understands that while they are identical, they are constantly sixfold; by means of this present [chapter]...
Chapter One: Only now do we know that the six stages are always identical. All four teachings discuss both nature and cultivation, and all discuss the six stages of identity.
One who thoroughly comprehends this principle has already mastered more than half of the Buddha’s teachings throughout his entire lifetime.
The Buddha said: "One who shaves off hair and beard to become a śramaṇa and receives the Way-dharma should renounce worldly wealth and possessions, begging for food until satisfied.
Eating but one meal at midday and staying overnight beneath a tree—be careful not to do these twice. That which causes people to be deluded and obscured is craving and desire."
This is the third chapter. It praises the superior practice of *dhūta* as the essential method for realizing the Way.
Since the preceding text stated that there is neither cultivation nor realization, there is a fear that people might misunderstand this and cling to the nature while abandoning cultivation;
therefore, I now specifically set forth the practice of shaking off worldly defilements (*dhūta*) as the means for severing desire and removing attachment. For example, although an ancient mirror...
The inherent luminosity must necessarily be polished and cleansed before it can attain brilliant purity.
The Buddha said: "Sentient beings perform ten things as good, and likewise ten things as evil. What are these ten? Three of the body, four of the mouth, and three of the mind.
The three of the body are killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. The four of the mouth are double-tongued speech, harsh speech, false speech," [and idle chatter].

Frivolous speech. The three mental [actions] are envy, malice, and delusion. These ten matters that do not accord with the Noble Path are called the ten unwholesome courses of action (*daśākuśalakarmapatha*).
If these evils are ceased, they are simply called the ten wholesome courses of action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*).
This is the fourth chapter. It clarifies that good and evil have no inherent nature; it is as easy as turning over one's hand.
Birth and death, as well as nirvana, consist solely of these three karmas and nothing else. To sever the life of another is called killing. To take what is not given is called stealing.
The mutual union of two is called sexual misconduct. To cause discord between others is called [slander].
Divisive speech, cursing, and reviling are called harsh speech. When the mind and mouth contradict one another, it is called false speech.
Meaningless and frivolous words are called idle chatter. Stinginess, meanness, greed, and intolerance of others' prosperity is termed envy.

Violence and cruelty, harboring resentment and binding oneself in anger, is termed *dveṣa* (hatred). To have no understanding of the principles of various phenomena and events is termed *moha* (delusion).
The seven branches of body and speech constitute solely the path of karma (*karmapatha*), while the three branches of the mental ground belong to the path of afflictions (*kleśamārga*).
Because one creates karma through delusion, one will inevitably encounter bitter fruits, remaining long bound within the three realms; therefore, this does not accord with the Noble Path.
If these evils cease, they are immediately termed the ten wholesome deeds (*daśa-kuśala*). It is like how dispelling darkness is itself light, or how melting ice results in water.

Now, since evil possesses both objective phenomena (*vastu*) and underlying principles (*nyāya*), the transformation of evil into good likewise possesses both phenomenal goodness and principled goodness.
Within phenomenal goodness, the lower grade of the ten wholesome deeds serves as the cause for the asuras; the middle grade...

The wholesome constitutes the cause for the human realm; the superior grade of the ten wholesome paths constitutes the cause for the heavenly realms. Within the wholesome according to principle, the wholesome of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is the cause for the two vehicles;
the wholesome of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is the cause for bodhisattvas; and the wholesome of the middle truth is the cause for the Buddha vehicle.
These three types of excellence are collectively termed the "superior-superior" (adhimātrādhimātra) ten wholesome paths of action.

This is because one who practices the excellence of conduct (*pratipattisampad*) does not necessarily attain the excellence of principle (*nyāyasampad*), whereas one who practices the excellence of principle necessarily possesses the perfection of the excellence of conduct.

The Buddha said: "If a person has many transgressions yet does not repent, and fails to suddenly still the mind, then sins will come upon the person like water flowing to the sea, gradually becoming deep and vast.

If a person has transgressions but understands their own error, reforms evil and practices good, then their sins will naturally be extinguished, just as a feverish illness is gradually cured through the breaking of a sweat."
This is the fifth chapter. Building upon the preceding intent to cease evil and practice good, it exhorts one to reform faults and transform toward virtue.

If one does not repent for one's transgressions, they will deepen and expand like water rushing to the sea. If one recognizes a fault and surely reforms, it is like inducing perspiration for an illness—the adventitious pathogens are naturally eliminated.
The Buddha said: "When wicked people hear of the good and thus come to cause disturbance, you should restrain yourself and remain free from anger or reproach.
It is those who come with evil intent who are themselves the ones who are wicked."
This sixth chapter clarifies that goodness can overcome evil, whereas evil cannot destroy goodness.
The preceding sections exhorted people to cease evil and practice good, and to reform their faults and turn toward virtue;

yet, fearing that foolish people might be intimidated by the harassment of wicked individuals and thus dare not act accordingly, this section warns them not to harbor anger or reproach such persons, for the evil resides solely with them.
This is because it has no connection with me. It is like an ugly face appearing in a clear mirror; that face is ugly by itself, but how could the mirror be ugly?
If one gives rise to anger and reproach for even a moment, one will instead take up that other's evil and make it one's own evil.
The Buddha said, "There are those who, upon hearing that I maintain the Way and practice great benevolence and compassion, proceed to revile me. The Buddha remained silent and did not respond.
When the reviling ceased, he asked, 'If you follow someone with courtesy and they do not accept it, does that courtesy return to you? He replied, 'It does.
The Buddha said, 'Now you have reviled me, and I have not accepted it; you are carrying this calamity back to your own person. It is just like..."
An echo responds to a sound; a shadow follows a form; in the end, there is no escaping this. Be careful not to do evil.
This is the seventh chapter, which serves as clear proof that those who come with evil intentions will themselves meet with evil.
Nowadays, when people hear abuse, few do not give rise to anger; this is very much like accepting a "thank-you note" and falling right into the abuser's trap.
Reflect on this, reflect on it! Someone asked: "Since the Buddha is so greatly compassionate, why does he not cause the abuser to be free from calamity?
The answer is: How could the Buddha wish for them to suffer calamity? It is simply that those people have brought calamity and affliction upon themselves. Now...
To admonish them to be careful not to do evil is to eliminate the source of their calamity; how profound is this compassion!
The Buddha said: "When an evil person harms a virtuous one, it is like spitting upward toward the sky. The spit does not reach the heavens, but falls back upon oneself."
When one raises dust against the wind, the dust does not reach its intended destination; instead, it returns to cloud the person's own body. The worthy cannot be defamed;

the resulting calamity will surely destroy oneself. This is the eighth chapter. It serves as a profound warning to the wicked not to harm the worthy, while simultaneously exhorting the worthy themselves.
If a person is truly virtuous, they are like the heavens or the high wind; how could they accept spit or dust? If one can be defiled by slander, they are not virtuous.
The Buddha said: "For one who is widely learned and loves the Way, the Way will surely be difficult to realize. For one who maintains their resolve and honors the Way, that Way is exceedingly great."
This is the ninth chapter. It exhorts those who receive the teachings to listen and reflect, and to reflect and practice;

one should not merely value learning that consists of mere words and hearsay. Those with extensive learning do not know how to enter contemplation according to the text, but instead strive only for the mechanical memorization of names and terms.
Those who love the Way do not realize that the source of the Way is none other than the mind itself, yet they falsely seek the Way outside of the mind.
Thus it is. Those who maintain their resolve direct every thought toward Bodhi, without mixing their minds with the pursuit of fame or profit.
Those who revere the Way embody the source of the mind in every thought, no longer seeking it outwardly.
The Buddha said, "When one sees a person practicing giving on the Path, to rejoice in and assist them brings forth exceedingly great merit. A śramaṇa asked, "Does this merit come to an end?
The Buddha said, "It is like a single torch; if hundreds or thousands of people each come with their own torches to take a portion from it,"
The cooked food has removed the darkness, yet this torch remains as it was; so too does the merit remain.
This is the tenth chapter, clarifying the merit of sympathetic joy (*anumodana*). It benefits both oneself and others, and its merit is inexhaustible. There are three kinds of giving:
first, the gift of material requisites (*āmiṣadāna*), which means alleviating poverty with wealth; second, the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*), which means...
Third is the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*), which means causing others to attain the four benefits through the three trainings (*triśikṣā*).

Not only does one gain immense merit by personally practicing these three kinds of giving, but even if one sees another practicing giving and assists them so that they may rejoice, one's merit is likewise inexhaustible.
[The passage] below, beginning with "Śramaṇa," clarifies a doubt: fearing that there might be foolish people who, while correctly practicing giving...
At that time, seeing others rejoice in his merit, he feared they would share in his own karmic reward; thus, he used a torch as before to enlighten them.

This was because not only would there be no decrease for him, but the meritorious retribution would become increasingly superior through such transmission. Long ago, there were two people gathering flowers;
one offered them to the Buddha himself, while the other gave them away to another person to offer to the Buddha. When asked about this by Maitreya, Maitreya said:
One who makes offerings for oneself alone attains the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha; one who gives to others attains unsurpassed Bodhi.

Indeed, delighting in solitude is not as good as sharing with others, and giving to a few is not as good as giving to the multitude. This is true without exception for both mundane and supramundane paths.
Cooked food is a metaphor for the attainment of the fruit of sainthood (*arhatship*). Dispelling darkness is a metaphor for destroying the three obstructions. The Buddha said:
"To feed a hundred evil people is not as good as feeding one virtuous person; to feed a thousand virtuous people is not as good as feeding one who upholds the five precepts;
to feed ten thousand who uphold the five precepts is not as good as feeding one *srotāpanna*; to feed a million *srotāpannas*..."
Feeding one *srotāpanna* is not as meritorious as feeding one *sakṛdāgāmin*. Feeding ten million *sakṛdāgāmins* is not as meritorious as feeding one *anāgāmin*.
Feeding one hundred million *anāgāmins* is not as meritorious as feeding one *arhat*. Feeding ten billion *arhats* is not as meritorious as feeding one *pratyekabuddha*.
Feeding one hundred billion *pratyekabuddhas* is not as meritorious as feeding one [Buddha] of the three periods of time.
To feed all the Buddhas of the three periods of time, numbering in the thousands of billions, is not as meritorious as feeding one who is without thought, without dwelling, without cultivation,
and without realization. This is the eleventh chapter, which compares the relative superiority and inferiority of fields of merit, enabling people to know where they should direct their devotion.
It is thus: one virtuous person surpasses a hundred evil people, which is evident and easy to understand.

As for the statement that "one who observes the five precepts surpasses a thousand virtuous people," this is because the ten wholesome deeds practiced by worldly virtuous people belong merely to the methods of the old physicians;

they do not take the Three Refuges as their essence and thus cannot constitute a bridge for transcending the world. If one can receive the threefold self-refuge and uphold the five [precepts], [they truly surpass them].

As a disciple of the Buddha, one understands the gates of the Four Noble Truths and the Four Foundations of Mindfulness; thus, within a single lifetime, one is capable of realizing the three fruits of the path.

For this reason, such a person is a thousand times superior to the common stream of beings. A *srotāpanna* (Stream-enterer) is ten thousand times superior to one who observes the five precepts, because the *srotāpanna* has already severed the delusions of views and has entered the ranks of the noble ones (*ārya*), thereby far surpassing both internal and external ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
Furthermore, one Sakṛdāgāmin surpasses ten million Srotāpannas. This is because the Sakṛdāgāmin has already severed the six grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) within the desire realm;

thus, their defilements have gradually thinned. Even if there were ten million Srotāpannas abiding in that fruit who had not yet cultivated the practice of superior progress, they would ultimately be unable to know the sphere of the second fruit, let alone reach it. One Arhat... [text continues]

An Anāgāmin surpasses ten million Srotāpannas. Since the Anāgāmin has already severed the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and brought them to an end, even ten million Srotāpannas could never know the sphere of the third fruit, much less reach it.
A single Arhat surpasses one hundred million Anāgāmins; "one hundred million" (*yi*) refers to ten thousand times ten thousand. An Arhat...

The Arhat has exhausted all views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and transcended the triple world; this is especially because they cannot be known by or reached by those who abide in the [lower] three fruits.

There are two kinds of Pratyekabuddhas: first, those who appear in an age when a Buddha exists, who receive the teaching of the twelve links of dependent origination, realize the Way, and attenuate their habitual tendencies;
these are called *Pratyekabuddhas* (Conditioned Awakened Ones). Second, those who appear in an age when no Buddha exists, who contemplate the illusory nature of phenomena...
Through transformation, they personally realize non-arising and sever the active afflictions (*kleśa*) along with their residual habits (*vāsanā*); thus they are called Pratyekabuddhas.
Since Arhats sever only the active afflictions, while Pratyekabuddhas sever both the active afflictions and their residual habits, a single Pratyekabuddha can surpass ten billion Arhats.
Regarding the Buddhas of the three periods of time, speaking in terms of the fruit of Buddhahood according to the *Pitaka*, it takes three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
By practicing the six perfections, one completely severs all habitual tendencies through correct cultivation and brings benefit to immeasurable sentient beings;

therefore, a single Buddha can surpass ten billion *pratyekabuddhas*. The phrase "one who is without thought, without dwelling, without cultivation, and without realization" refers to those from the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) upward, and may also encompass the first ground of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*) and the Buddha-ground of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*). This is because...

The Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) takes form as its substance and enters into emptiness; knowing that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, it realizes that mindfulness is non-mindfulness, abiding is non-abiding, cultivation is non-cultivation, and realization is non-realization.

Upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood, one is able to manifest a most towering body in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, reigning as sovereign over the three thousandfold world system. This distinguishes it from the Stage of Joy (Prāmodyabhūmi) of the Separate Teaching, wherein [the Bodhisattva] fully awakens.

Their minds abide [in suchness], and they have all already partially realized the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). They are all capable of manifesting as Buddhas within the hundred realms and displaying the eight phases of attaining enlightenment.
Therefore, making offerings to this single person is superior to making offerings to a thousand billion Buddhas of the three periods of time.

Furthermore, the preceding eight instances were all based on the field [of merit]; this ninth instance is based on the mind. This is because [the previous cases] had not yet reached the realization of the One.
All dharmas are fundamentally without thought; they abide in fundamental non-abiding; they are cultivated in fundamental non-cultivation; they are realized in fundamental non-realization.

Therefore, within the dharma of equality, one distinguishes between superior and inferior. If one thoroughly understands the wondrous principle of no-thought, no-abiding, no-cultivation, and no-realization, then from the lowliest evildoer up to all Buddhas, there are none who are not without thought and without abiding.

There is no distinction between one who practices without cultivation and one who realizes without realization; therefore, when a person offers food to a Buddha and the Buddha gives it to a starving dog, their merit is no different.
Thus, Vimalakīrti offered one portion to the Tathāgata Duṣprasaha and gave the other portion to the lowliest beggar in the fields.
Merit is also equal. If one does not know the distinctions between the superiority and inferiority of merit, there is no means by which to manifest the preciousness of cultivating virtue.
If one does not realize that sentient beings and Buddhas are fundamentally equal from the outset, there is no means by which to awaken to the source of the nature’s virtues.
This is called "always identical yet always distinct; always distinct yet always identical"—the subtle dharma-gate of the natural order of the *dharmadhātu*.

The Buddha said: "There are twenty difficulties for human beings: it is difficult to practice giving while poor; it is difficult to study the Way while of noble status; it is difficult to sacrifice one's life when facing certain death;

it is difficult to encounter the Buddhist scriptures; it is difficult to be born during the era of a Buddha; it is difficult to endure the temptations of form and desire; it is difficult to not seek after things even when seeing what is beautiful;

it is difficult to remain free from anger when insulted; it is difficult to refrain from using one's power when one possesses it; it is difficult to be without attachment to affairs as they arise; it is difficult to study extensively and widely..."

The difficulty of thorough investigation; the difficulty of eliminating the conceit of "I"; the difficulty of not disparaging those who have not yet studied; the difficulty of maintaining equanimity in thought and conduct; the difficulty of refraining from speaking of right and wrong;
the difficulty of meeting virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); the difficulty of realizing one's nature and studying the Way; the difficulty of following along to transform and save others;
the difficulty of remaining unmoved when encountering external objects; and the difficulty of skillfully understanding expedient means (*upāya*).
This is the twelfth chapter. It briefly sets forth twenty difficult matters as an exhortation. To act in accordance with one's inclinations is easy; to act contrary to them is difficult.
However, if one can deeply arouse a resolute mind, then even what is difficult becomes easy.
If, on the other hand, one merely follows worldly customs, then even what is easy becomes difficult. Indeed, for those in poverty, practicing generosity is difficult; therefore, even a small amount—
If one grants permission for such giving, the merit obtained is exceedingly great; thus, one must not fail to exert effort.

Yet, we see in the present those who are poor yet capable of giving, while the wealthy, on the contrary, are unwilling to give—how then can their stinginess and baseness be described? When those of noble rank and high status study the Way, their practice of giving may be inferred from this principle.
That which people value most highly is their own bodies and lives; if one can truly renounce one’s life, then what [is there that cannot be given]?
While it is true that there are things one cannot achieve, I have never heard of anyone who cherishes their life and fears death yet has actually attained longevity and immortality;
if such a thing were possible, why would one begrudge anything? Buddhist scriptures are difficult to encounter;

now that you have fortunately encountered them, if you do not investigate them with refined diligence and exhaust your thoughts, how is this any different from not having encountered them at all? A Buddha’s era is difficult to meet; now that you have fortunately met a Buddha’s era—
If one does not apply oneself to cultivation at the proper time, how is this any different from never encountering [the opportunity] at all?

Although sensual desire is what ordinary people constantly crave, if one examines it and perceives that its flavor is meager while its suffering is abundant, or observes it as being like an illusion or a shadow, then how could it be difficult to endure and restrain?
If, upon seeing something desirable, one knows that it cannot necessarily be obtained, then the greedy mind will naturally subside. If one is...
When insulted, simply exercise forbearance through the emotions and dismiss it through reason; then the intent of anger will naturally subside.

Regard wealth and status as dew upon the tips of blades of grass—how could one allow power to be used to overawe others? View all circumstances and objects as mere conditions within a dream—why must one weary the mind with schemes and arrangements?
To study extensively without investigating deeply is like entering the ocean without a compass; how can one thereby comprehend the underlying principle? Relying [on such superficiality]...
To study and yet give rise to conceit is like irrigating fertile soil to nourish weeds; it instead harms the fine grain. The Buddha once spoke of four things that must not be disregarded:
first, fire, though small, must not be disregarded; second, a dragon, though small, must not be disregarded;
third, a prince, though young, must not be disregarded; fourth, a śramaṇa, though junior, must not be disregarded.
Alas! There are those today who treat learning lightly because they do not yet understand that it must not be neglected.
When the mind is impartial, the merit of giving to the Tathāgata Duṣprasaha is no different from the merit of giving to the lowliest beggar.

When one has obliterated the distinction between right and wrong, then all phenomena are nothing other than the Buddha-dharma. As long as one has not forgotten the emotional views of right and wrong, one will certainly be unable to see the Dharma.
O true spiritual friend, if one does not perceive the true nature of the single thought-moment before one, it is absolutely impossible to study the Unsurpassed Way.
Without studying the provisional and ultimate paths that accord with this nature, one cannot transform and deliver others according to their needs.
If one has not yet mastered the skillful means for transforming and delivering others, how can one remain unmoved by a single mind while beholding the realms of the ten dharma-realms?

If one cannot fully perceive the phenomena and principles of all dharma-realms within each individual dharma-realm, by what means could one skillfully understand the expedient means of their identical essence?
Therefore, it is known that among these twenty matters, each subsequent one is more difficult than the preceding.
A śramaṇa asked the Buddha, "By what causes and conditions can one know past lives and realize the ultimate Way? The Buddha said, "Purify the mind and maintain one's resolve;

thus one may realize the ultimate Way. It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is removed, its brightness remains. By severing desire and having no cravings, one shall attain knowledge of past lives."
This is the thirteenth chapter. The intent of the question lies primarily in past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*), while the intent of the answer lies primarily in realizing the Way (*mārga*).
For one who knows their past lives does not necessarily realize the Ultimate Way; yet one who realizes the Ultimate Way is certainly able to know their past lives.
A śramaṇa asked the Buddha, "What is good? What is greatest? The Buddha said, "To practice the Way and maintain the truth is good;
for one's will to be in harmony with the Way is greatest."
This is the fourteenth chapter. It clarifies that among all forms of goodness, nothing is more excellent than true cultivation; and among all things, nothing is greater than actual realization.
If one practices the Way while guarding the truth, then all myriad virtues will converge. If one’s resolve merges with the Way, then the essence of the Dharma-realm becomes perfect and complete.

A śramaṇa asked the Buddha, "What possesses great strength? What is most luminous? The Buddha said: "Patience possesses great strength, for it harbors no malice and is further endowed with peace and well-being.

One who practices patience is free from evil and will surely become honored among men. When the defilements of the mind are extinguished and purified of all blemish, this is what constitutes being most luminous.
From the time before heaven and earth existed until this very day, throughout all the ten directions, there has never been..."
There is nothing he does not see; there is nothing he does not know; there is nothing he does not hear. Having attained all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), he may be called truly enlightened.
This fifteenth chapter clarifies that the power of patience (*kṣānti*) is great, that it extinguishes defilements, and that its clarity is far-reaching. There are three kinds of patience.

First is the patience of enduring enmity and harm, also called the patience toward sentient beings (*sattvakṣānti*). Second is the patience of accepting suffering, also called the patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*).
Third is the patience of discerning the Dharma, also called the patience regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārthakṣānti*). Here, one enters the ultimate truth by means of enduring enmity and harm.
The remainder of the text is easy to understand.
The Buddha said: "Those who harbor desire and do not see the Way are like clear water that has been stirred by hand;
though many people gather around it, none can see their own reflections. Because people’s minds are turbid due to the entanglement of desire, they do not see the Way.
You śramaṇas, you should abandon desire. When the defilement of desire is exhausted, the Way will become visible."
This is the sixteenth chapter. It clarifies that the water of our own human mind is fundamentally clear; this is itself the Ultimate Way (*zhìdào*).
However, because it is stirred by craving and desire, one cannot manifest the images of the ten realms within a single thought-moment.

If one abandons the craving and desire of the triple world, the defilements of view and thought are exhausted, and the Path of True Reality (*zhēndì*) can be seen. If one abandons the craving for partial truth, the dust...

When the defilement of dust is exhausted, the path of the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) becomes visible. When the craving for karmic retribution and the defilement of ignorance are exhausted, the path of the middle truth (madhyama-satya) becomes visible.
The Buddha said: "As for one who perceives the Path, it is like holding a torch and entering a dark chamber; the darkness is immediately extinguished, and the light alone remains.
When one studies the Path and perceives the Truths, ignorance is immediately extinguished, and clarity remains forever."
This is the seventeenth chapter. It profoundly reveals that ignorance has no intrinsic nature; therefore, it can be eternally extinguished upon the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
It also reveals that as long as ignorance is not extinguished, one cannot be said to have attained the True Path of Seeing.

Knowing that ignorance is capable of being extinguished prevents the arising of despondency, while knowing that the True Path of Seeing is ever-luminous allows one to eliminate overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

The Buddha said: "In my Dharma, mindfulness is without the act of mindful recollection; practice is without the act of practicing; speech is without the act of speaking; cultivation is without the act of cultivating.
Those who realize this are near; those who are deluded are far. The path of words is severed, and it is not constrained by material things. To err by even a hair’s breadth—"
To lose this for even a moment is a great error.
This is the eighteenth chapter, which clarifies that the cultivation of mindful practice and speech transcends both the gates of existence and non-existence;

thus, one must not allow the emotional views of existence or non-existence to settle upon them. Mindfulness is itself non-mindfulness; therefore, one should constantly maintain mindfulness of this non-mindfulness.
Consider this: how could it be that non-thought constitutes "no-thought"? The three phrases beginning with "practice" can be understood by analogy with this.

If one realizes this, then every encounter with phenomena is entirely the truth; for the deluded, however, they move further and further away. The characteristics of language are themselves the characteristics of liberation.
Therefore, the path of language is cut off; all things are the very nature of True Suchness (tathatā), and thus are not constrained by material objects.

To involve oneself even slightly in existence or non-existence is to create a gulf as vast as heaven and earth. Thus, to err by even a hair’s breadth, or to involve oneself in discursive thought, immediately results in superfluous dharmas.
Therefore, it is lost in an instant.
The Buddha said: "Contemplate heaven and earth, and reflect upon impermanence; contemplate the world, and reflect upon impermanence; contemplate the numinous awakening, and that is itself bodhi."
When one understands it in this way, the attainment of the Way is swift.
This is the nineteenth chapter, which clarifies the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*), expelling the false to preserve the real. Heaven covers above and earth bears below.

Ordinary people reckon that things are permanent and substantially existent. Now, observing the heavens, we see that cold and heat alternate; observing the earth, we see that hills and valleys shift and change.
Since such phenomena are subject to arising and ceasing and lack permanence, how could they be real dharmas existing apart from the mind? Next, observe within one’s own body:

"time" (adhvan) refers to the flow of succession, and "directions" (dis) refer to spatial orientation. Time is certainly never stationary from moment to moment, and the directions likewise [are not fixed].
There is no fixed nature; how could there be a real self or real dharmas therein? This dispels the fundamental emptiness of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).

Next, one contemplates the nature of the numinous awareness of the present single thought-moment. Since it is already free from the two attachments to self and dharmas, it immediately becomes the four wisdoms of enlightenment (*bodhi*).
This preserves the reality of the dependent and perfected natures (*paratantra* and *pariniṣpanna*). By dispelling the empty, there is no superimposition (*samāropa*).
This is slander. To maintain reality, there is no slander of diminution. Being neither existent nor non-existent, one swiftly accords with the Middle Way.
The Buddha said: "One should contemplate that within the body, the four great elements each have their own names, yet none possess a self. Since a self is entirely absent,"
"It is merely like an illusion.
This is the twentieth chapter, which shows people how to contemplate the body through the four great elements and thereby enter the Dharma-gate of the illusory nature.
That which is solid within the body is called earth; that which is moist is called water; that which is warm is called fire; and that which is mobile is called wind. Seek [them].

I am ultimately unattainable. Both the subject that accomplishes and the object accomplished are in essence like an illusion; the subject that contemplates and the object contemplated are likewise like an illusion.
Through this single analogy of illusion, one may penetrate the principles of emptiness, the provisional, and the Middle Way.
Thus, we know that the contemplation of the body through the four great elements is truly the general gateway to the Four Teachings.
The Buddha said: "People follow their passions in pursuit of fame and reputation. When their fame becomes prominent, the body has already perished.

To covet the enduring fame of this world without studying the Way is to labor in vain and exhaust one's form. It is like burning incense: although people smell the fragrance, the incense itself has been consumed;
yet the fire that endangered the body remains behind."
This is the twenty-first chapter. It clearly demonstrates that those who seek fame and reputation not only derive no benefit, but rather suffer great harm.
The Buddha said: "Wealth and sensual pleasure are things that people cannot renounce; they are like honey on the edge of a blade—insufficient for even a single meal."
Its flavor is exquisite; yet if a small child licks it, they suffer the calamity of having their tongue cut off.
This twenty-second chapter clearly demonstrates that the taste of wealth and sensual beauty is meager while the harm they inflict is immense.
A person of wisdom must not resemble such a small child.

The Buddha said: "People are bound by their wives, children, and homes more tightly than they are in prison. While there is a time for release from prison, there is no thought of separation from one's wife and children.
When one is emotionally attached to sensual forms, how could one fear the toil of pursuing them? Even when faced with the peril of a tiger’s mouth, the mind remains contentedly submissive.
One throws oneself into the mud and drowns; therefore, such a person is called an ordinary man (*pṛthagjana*). Only by penetrating this gate can one emerge from the net of worldly dust."
Han. This is the twenty-third chapter. It clearly elucidates how wives, children, and dwellings bury people [in saṃsāra], and exhorts one to distance oneself from them quickly.
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), men and women as well as kinsmen constitute "wives and children," while various palaces constitute [the dwelling].
The realm of form takes the savor of dhyāna as its wife and children, and the four dhyāna heavens as its house and home.

The formless realm takes the concentration of delusion as its wife and children, and the four formless heavens as its house and home. Devoured by craving and views, the affliction is like that of a tiger’s maw.
To speak by extending this analogy: the followers of the Two Vehicles take the savor of a single liberation as their wife and children, and the partial truth of *nirvāṇa* as their house and home.
The provisional teachings take the practice of supernatural powers as one's wife and children, while entering the mundane world from the truth is taken as one's home.
Only when one has penetrated both the gates of emptiness and existence does one achieve the fruit of the Middle Way and non-arising.
The Buddha said: "Among all forms of craving, none is more profound than that for physical form (*rūpa*). As for this desire for form, it is so vast that there is nothing beyond it.
Fortunately, it exists as a single entity; were it to be doubled, not a single person throughout the heavens would be able to practice the Way."
This is the twenty-fourth chapter, which deeply clarifies that sensual desire is a grave illness for sentient beings. The *Buddhāvatamsaka-sūtra* states:
"If the lustful mind is not eliminated, one cannot transcend the mundane dust."
The Buddha said: "A person driven by desire is like one who holds a torch while walking against the wind; there will inevitably be the calamity of burning their hand.
This twenty-fifth chapter clearly demonstrates that desire must not be cultivated or approached. When holding a torch against the wind, there is no one who does not burn their hand;
how then could one who cultivates and approaches desire fail to damage the pure Dharma-body? It is harmful.
"Is this the hand of skillful means?
A heavenly deity offered a jade maiden to the Buddha, wishing to corrupt his resolve. The Buddha said, "A leather bag filled with various impurities—what have you come here for?

Begone; I have no need of you. The deity’s reverence increased all the more, and he consequently asked about the meaning of the Way. The Buddha explained it for him, and [the deity] immediately attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The Fruit of Stream-entry.
This is the twenty-sixth chapter. It clarifies that the Buddha was not disturbed by Māra, and was thus able to convert him. The "heavenly deity" refers to Māra Pāpīyān.
When the Buddha first attained enlightenment, Māra first raised his armored troops, but they were unable to harm the Buddha. Next...
She offered her three daughters, yet they were still unable to disturb the Buddha. They then returned to him, were transformed by his teaching, and realized the first fruit of the path (srotāpatti).
If a person can contemplate those women as a leather bag filled with various impurities, lustful thoughts will be eliminated; thus, both self and others will benefit.
The Buddha said: "One who practices the Way is like a piece of wood floating on water, following the current as it flows. It does not touch either bank;
it is not taken by people, nor obstructed by ghosts or spirits, nor held back by eddies, nor does it rot.
I guarantee that this wood will certainly reach the sea. So too is the person who studies the Way: they are not deluded by sensual desires, nor are they [overcome] by various evils..."
Harassed by these, one must practice diligence and non-action; I guarantee that such a person will surely attain the Way.
This is the twenty-seventh chapter, which uses metaphors to clarify that those who study the Way must remain far removed from all obstacles.

The two banks serve as a metaphor for emotional desires—namely, the emotional desires of views and afflictions (*kleśa*), and the emotional desires of ignorance (*avidyā*). As for the emotional desires of views and afflictions, they involve deep attachment and defilement.
Birth and death are like touching this shore; ignorance and sensual desire, which lead to attachment to nirvana, are like touching the other shore.
Humans and ghosts represent the various heterodox paths. Being entangled in the net of craving is like being captured by men; being shrouded by the net of false views is likewise so described.
As if obstructed by ghosts and spirits, one remains caught in a whirlpool, which is the direct opposite of diligence. To be corrupt is the direct opposite of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is because one is unable to maintain a straightforward mind and right mindfulness toward True Suchness (*tathatā*);

though always desiring to advance, one instead regresses, like a current that flows swiftly only to turn back into a whirlpool. Failing to reach the dharma-nature of the unconditioned, one’s cultivation of merit and wisdom remains attached to signs (*nimitta*).

In the end, it will surely become putrid and decayed. Therefore, one must certainly not be deluded by the passions of birth-and-death or nirvana, nor be vexed by the various evils of craving and false views.

One should apply oneself with diligence while maintaining right mindfulness of True Suchness (*tathatā*), fully realizing that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
"Then one may attain the Way and preserve it.
The Buddha said: "Be careful not to trust your own mind; your own mind is not to be trusted. Be careful not to associate with forms;
when you associate with forms, calamity arises. Only after you have attained arhatship may you trust your own mind."
This is the twenty-eighth chapter. It provides a profound admonition that the mind-horse is difficult to tame and that one should avoid the calamities of sensory forms (*rūpa*).
Since beginningless time, sentient beings have merely indulged their passions and followed their whims, enduring saṃsāra for a long time without realizing arhatship.
Constantly accompanied by ignorance (*avidyā*), craving, views, and pride, how can you trust your own minds and fail to exercise diligent investigation?
"Is it so? The Buddha said, "Be careful not to look upon the forms of women, nor speak with them. If you must speak with them, maintain a correct mind and reflect:
'I am a śramaṇa dwelling in a turbid world; I should be like a lotus flower, unsullied by the mud. Contemplate those who are old."

Toward those who are like mothers, those of equal age like elder sisters, the younger like younger sisters, and the very young like one's own children, one should give rise to a mind of deliverance and extinguish evil thoughts.
This is the twenty-ninth chapter, which clarifies the expedient means for guarding against transgressions by keeping distant from women, thereby giving rise to goodness and extinguishing evil.
Furthermore, first one should expect oneself to be unstained like a lotus flower; this is self-benefit through right mindfulness.
Then, one regards others as a mother, a sister, a younger sister, or a child and delivers them to liberation; this is benefiting others through a compassionate heart.
Since one thus accords with these two benefits, evil thoughts will naturally subside and cease.
The Buddha said: "One who practices the Way is like dry grass; when fire approaches, it must be avoided. When a practitioner of the Way encounters desire, he must certainly distance himself from it.
This is the thirtieth chapter, which extends the admonition to remain far removed from all desires, lest one be burned and harmed by the fire of desire."
Furthermore, the six sense faculties are like dry grass, and the six sensory objects are likened to a raging fire.
Before the mind and its objects have both become empty, one should practice the sublime conduct of detachment.

The Buddha said: "There was a man who suffered from unrestrained lust and wished to remove his own genitals. The Buddha said to him: 'If you were to cut off your genitals, it would not be as good as cutting off the mind.
The mind is like the chief minister; if the chief minister stops, all the attendants cease their activity. As long as the depraved mind does not stop, [the afflictions will continue to arise]."
"What benefit is there in severing the aggregates? The Buddha spoke this verse for him: "Desire arises within your mind; the mind arises through conceptualization.
When both minds are each stilled, they are neither form nor mental formations. The Buddha said, "This verse was spoken by Kāśyapa Buddha."
This is the thirty-first chapter. It clarifies that the severing of desire must be severed from the mind. As for the method of severing the mind:
one investigates that this desire arises from the *manas* (the faculty of intention); the *manas*, in turn, arises from conceptualization (*saṃjñā*).
Is this conceptualization self-generated, generated by another, generated by both together, or generated without cause? Furthermore, does this conceptualization exist within?
Is it outside? Is it in between the two? Does it exist in the past, the present, or the future?
When one investigates in this manner, discursive thought becomes tranquil. Because discursive thought is tranquil, the mind becomes tranquil.
Because the mind is tranquil, desire becomes tranquil. Because desire is tranquil, one contemplates all forms as being like reflections in a mirror and so forth. Thus...
This is not form. To contemplate all conditioned phenomena as being like foam and bubbles is itself non-conditioned.
This has been transmitted successively from the Buddhas of the past; it is nothing other than the transmission of these very skillful means for taming the mind.
The Buddha said: "From craving and desire arise sorrow; from sorrow arises fear. If one is detached from craving, what sorrow and what fear can there be?
This is the thirty-second chapter, which traces the origin of sorrow and fear to craving and desire, and exhorts people to sever desire and abandon craving.
Since beginningless time, sentient beings have falsely identified the four great elements as their own self-nature and have falsely identified the six... [senses].

The shadows of worldly conditions are the manifestations of one's own mind; yet, through attachment and craving, one refuses to relinquish them even for a moment, thereby giving rise to all manner of anxieties and afflictions, as well as all manner of terrors.

One should contemplate the body by means of the four elements to know that the body is without self, and contemplate the mind by means of the four modes of activity to know that the mind is impermanent.
