Once desire and craving are severed, anxiety and fear will naturally vanish.
The Buddha said: "Now, one who practices the Way is like a single man fighting ten thousand men. He dons his armor and goes forth from his gate;
yet his mind may become timid and weak, or he may retreat halfway, or he may die in the fray, or he may emerge victorious and return.
A śramaṇa who studies the Way should likewise firmly maintain his resolve, being diligent, courageous, and sharp, fearing no objective realm before him, so as to destroy all māras."
One attains the fruits of the Path.
This is the thirty-third chapter. It uses analogies to clarify that those who seek the Path must possess precepts, concentration, and wisdom.

The mind that applies itself with single-minded diligence to learning the Path is like a person [who, despite] beginningless false delusions and the habitual tendencies of various afflictions, is like...
Ten thousand people receive and uphold the pure precepts as if donning armor; by steadfastly maintaining their minds, they are free from any sense of cowardice—this is the power of morality (*śīla*).
Through diligent vigor and sharp resolve, they do not retreat halfway—this is the power of concentration (*samādhi*).
By not fearing the objects before them, they do not engage in combat to the point of death—this is the power of wisdom (*prajñā*). When these three powers are united, [they are complete].
Having destroyed the countless demons from time immemorial and realized the fruit of the Way, he returned as a victor.
A śramaṇa was reciting the *Kāśyapa-buddha-śāsana-sūtra* at night; his voice was mournful and strained, and he was filled with regret and the desire to withdraw.
The Buddha asked him, "When you were formerly a householder, what was your occupation? He replied, "I loved playing the lute. The Buddha said, "If the strings are too slack..."
"What? he asked. He replied, "It does not sound. "What if the strings are too tight? He replied, "The sound is cut off. "What if they are adjusted to the middle ground between tight and loose?
He replied, "All the notes are harmonious. The Buddha said, "It is the same for a śramaṇa practicing the Way.
If the mind is properly tuned, the Way can be attained. If one is violent toward the Way, one becomes exhausted; when the body is exhausted, the mind gives rise to affliction. The mind—

If one gives rise to vexation, one's practice will immediately regress. Once practice has regressed, retribution for offenses will surely be added. Only by maintaining a pure and tranquil path can one avoid losing it.
This is the thirty-fourth chapter, clarifying the method of studying the Way: one must skillfully regulate body and mind, and not allow them to become lax.

This is because one has suddenly lost what was attained. Confucian scholars also say, "Those who advance with excessive haste will retreat with equal speed," and they further say, "Do not forget, do not force.
Such are the essential principles for the three vehicles.
The Buddha said: "It is like a person forging iron; by removing the dross, it is formed into a vessel, and the vessel becomes refined and excellent. So too for one who studies the Way:
by removing the defilements of the mind, their practice becomes pure."
This is the thirty-fifth chapter. It uses a parable to clarify that defilements must be eliminated. By merely removing defilements, one achieves purity;
that is to say, simply exhaust all mundane sentiments, for there is no separate "sage-understanding" apart from this. There is only the method for removing the cataracts.
There is no dharma other than luminosity itself. In becoming a Buddha or founding a patriarchal lineage, how could there be any dharma to be attained apart from the mind?
It is nothing more than the thorough purification of habitual tendencies.
The Buddha said: "It is difficult for a person to escape the evil realms and obtain human birth. Having obtained human birth, it is difficult to be male rather than female.

Having obtained male status, it is difficult for the six sense faculties to be complete. Having the six faculties complete, it is difficult to be born in a central land. Having been born in a central land,"
It is difficult to encounter the era of a Buddha. Having encountered the era of a Buddha, it is difficult to meet with the Way. Having met with the Way, it is difficult to give rise to faith.
Having given rise to faith, it is difficult to resolve upon bodhicitta. Having resolved upon bodhicitta, it is difficult to practice without cultivation and realize without attainment.
This is the thirty-sixth chapter. It successively clarifies matters that are difficult to encounter in order to deeply admonish people, so that they do not lose this excellent opportunity.
If one does not realize that there is neither cultivation nor realization, how can one be said to have truly awakened the bodhicitta?
If one does not awaken true bodhicitta, how can it be called faith? If one does not give rise to faith, how can it be called encountering the Way? Since this is not the case...
What benefit is there in encountering the Way or meeting a Buddha? If meeting them is equivalent to not meeting them, then the Central Kingdom is no different from the borderlands.
If the Central Kingdom is no different from the borderlands, then having the six sense-faculties complete is no different from having them incomplete.
If having the six sense-faculties complete is no different from having them incomplete, then even a man is not truly a man. If a man does not constitute a man, then what is a human body?

Distinguish yourself from the evil realms. Reflect quietly on this: how could one not resolve to generate the bodhicitta and urgently awaken to the essential principle that there is neither cultivation nor realization? The Buddha said:
"O Son of the Buddha, even if you are thousands of li away from me, if you keep my precepts in mind, you will surely attain the fruit of the Way. [He] is at my left side.
Although one may constantly see me as described above, if they do not comply with my precepts, they will ultimately fail to attain the Way.
This is the thirty-seventh chapter. It clarifies deeply that [the distance] is near when the mind is near, and distant when the mind is distant;

it is not by means of physical traces that one judges nearness or distance. Such are the sincere words from the Golden Mouth regarding the gravity of the precepts. What shall the disciples of the final age do?

Why do you not reflect? The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: In the kingdom of Pārāśī, there were two bhikṣus who traveled together as companions to Śrāvastī to pay their respects to the World-Honored One.
On the way, they became exhausted with thirst and found no water. Upon reaching a well, one bhikṣu drew water and drank it immediately.
The other bhikṣu examined the water and saw insects; he did not drink. The bhikṣu who had drunk the water asked him:
[The man] said, "Why do you not drink? He replied, "The World-Honored One has established a precept that one must not drink water containing insects.

The other urged him again, saying, "Venerable sir, simply drink; do not let yourself die of thirst so that you may not see the Buddha. He replied, "I would rather lose my life than violate the Buddha’s precepts.
Thereupon, he died of thirst and was immediately reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where his celestial body was fully perfected.
That night, he arrived first at the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at his feet, and heard the Dharma, whereby he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
The monk who had drunk the water arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling on a later day. The Buddha, knowing this, asked him intentionally: "Where have you come from? Did you have companions?
He then answered with the aforementioned account. The Buddha said, "Foolish man! You did not see me, yet you thought you had seen me. That [other] one has died."

“Monks, there are those who have already seen me before. If a monk is negligent and indolent, failing to restrain his sense faculties, then even though he dwells in the same place as me, he is far from me; though he sees me, I do not see him. But if there is a monk...”
On the further shore of the ocean, those who are heedful, diligent and tireless, and who restrain their sense faculties—though they may be far from me, I always see them; they are always near to me.
The Buddha asked a śramaṇa, "In what interval does a person's life reside? He replied, "In several days. The Buddha said, "You do not yet know the Way.
He then asked another śramaṇa, "In what interval does a person's life reside? He replied, "In the interval of a meal. The Buddha said, "You do not yet know the Way.
He then asked another śramaṇa, "In what interval does a person's life reside? He replied, "In the interval of a single breath. The Buddha said, "Excellent!"
You have understood the Way.
This, the thirty-eighth chapter, clarifies that human life is impermanent; it is essential not to remain ignorant of this.

The continuous, uninterrupted connection of form and mind throughout a single lifetime is called the "life-faculty" (jīvitendriya). It is a provisional designation based upon the seeds of the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), and is not a substantial entity.
This is the nature of reality: although the exhalation has entered, the inhalation is difficult to preserve; how much more so for that which arises and ceases moment by moment, thought after thought!
Were it not for profound reflection and discerning contemplation, how could one possibly know this? Formerly, there was a king in the Western Regions who did not believe in the Buddha-dharma.
He asked a patriarch, "I have seen the various ascetic practices of the non-Buddhists, yet they were still unable to subdue their lust."
"Your Majesty, the four requisites for a śramaṇa are now provided according to his wishes; how could he possibly sever his afflictions? The Patriarch said, "Your Majesty, try this:
take a prisoner from among those condemned to die in prison, fill a vessel with oil, and have him hold it in his hands.
Then, station four executioners behind him with their blades drawn. If he can keep even a single drop from spilling, his crime shall be pardoned. But if he spills even one—"
A drop fell. He cut it off with his hand. They then went together to the crossroads. The king further sent out all his palace women and musicians to dance and sing everywhere.

He asked the culprit what he had seen and heard. Following these instructions, the king had one of the culprits carry a bowl full of oil in his hands as he passed through the midst of the four crossroads and the throngs of women and musicians; not a single drop fell. Consequently, the king pardoned him.
Regarding his crime, the king summoned him and questioned him: "What did you see or hear at the crossroads?

The criminal replied, "At that time, I was only afraid that a single drop of oil might fall; with a sharp blade pressed against my neck, I saw nothing but the oil in my hand, and perceived nothing else.
The Patriarch said to the king, "He was merely sparing this one body from death."

Consequently, he perceived neither form nor sound; how much less could a śramaṇa, upholding the Buddha’s supreme teaching of impermanence and non-self, fail to feel deep compassion for the suffering of birth and death throughout immeasurable kalpas? How could he not sever his afflictions?
Those heterodox practitioners, ignorant of impermanence and non-self, merely engage in ascetic practices; thus, they are of no benefit. Thereupon, the king believed.

I am moved to sigh. Truly, one must know that human life exists but between inhalation and exhalation. Why wait until a butcher follows with a knife in hand before the mind finally becomes free from negligence?
The Buddha said: "Those who study the Buddha-way should believe and comply with all that the Buddha has spoken. It is like eating honey;
it is sweet both in the center and at the edges. My sutras are likewise."
This is the thirty-ninth chapter. It clarifies that all Buddhist scriptures should be believed and followed;

one must not arbitrarily differentiate between the Great and Small Vehicles or the Sudden and Gradual teachings, thereby giving rise to feelings of superiority or inferiority. The Buddha’s verbal teachings do not transcend the provisional and the real:

he established the provisional for the sake of the real, and opened the provisional to reveal the real. Within each of the four teachings, there are four gates, and each gate possesses the four *siddhāntas*. Now, there is...

To cling to the small while slandering the great; to cling to the great while slandering the small; to cling to phenomena while repudiating principle; or to cling to principle while repudiating phenomena—all these are in violation of the Buddha’s intent.
The Buddha said: "A śramaṇa practicing the Way should not be like a 'grinding ox. Though its body moves along the path, its mind does not practice the Way. As for the mind's Way...
"If one merely practices [external forms], what is the use of practicing the Way?
This is the fortieth chapter, clarifying that the practice of the Way lies in the mind and not in outward form.
If the mind does not enter the Way, to labor in external rituals in vain—how is this any different from a worn-out ox?
The Buddha said: "One who practices the Way is like an ox carrying a heavy load through deep mud; exhausted, it does not dare look left or right.
Only after emerging from the mud can it find rest. A śramaṇa should contemplate that sensual desires are even more perilous than that mud."
By maintaining a straightforward mind and recollecting the Way, one may escape suffering.
This is Chapter Forty-one. It admonishes people to maintain a straightforward mind and recollect the Way, taking the transcendence of sensual desires as their goal.
The Buddha said: "I regard the rank of kings and nobles as dust passing through a crack;
I regard treasures of gold and jade as shards and pebbles; I regard garments of fine silk as worn-out rags; I regard the great trichiliocosm as a single *kośamba* fruit;
I regard the waters of Lake Anavatapta as oil for anointing the feet; I regard the gates of skillful means as a heap of conjured jewels; and I regard the Unsurpassed Vehicle as gold seen in a dream."
Bai regarded the Buddha-way as flowers before one's eyes; he regarded meditative concentration as a pillar of Mount Sumeru; he regarded nirvana as waking from sleep after day and night;

he regarded the inverted and the correct as the dance of the six dragons; he regarded equality as the ground of true reality; and he regarded the flourishing of transformation as the trees of the four seasons.

This is the forty-second chapter. It concludes by clarifying how the Buddha-eye and other [perceptions] contemplate all phenomena, thereby destroying the sentient beings' clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
One hundred years among humans do not exceed a single day and night in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
A single great kalpa of the Sahā world does not exceed a single day and night in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Thus, what difference is there between the glory and nobility of kings and lords and the dust that passes through a crack? The vessels of the various heavens are made entirely of the seven treasures; the ground of the Land of Ultimate Bliss is composed of gold.
When Maitreya attains the Way of the Buddha, this very ground shall likewise be made of lapis lazuli, let alone being made of jade, gold, or clay.
Gravel and such are all composed of the four subtle elements; what is there to value in them? Though one’s clothing may be of fine silk, it serves no purpose other than to cover the body.
If it can merely conceal one's shame, what harm is there in tattered cloth? The Great Trichiliocosm is likewise "mind-only," and a single mustard seed is also "mind-only.
When observing their appearances, they are fundamentally illusory; thus, within this state, one arbitrarily calculates size and magnitude. When observing their nature, it is fundamentally true.
The mind that transforms the great trichiliocosm is neither large nor many; the mind that transforms a single myrobalan fruit is neither small nor few.
This may be understood by analogy with the waters of Lake Anavatapta and the oil for anointing the feet.

As for the "gateways of skillful means," these are the various expedients established by the Buddhas—the three vehicles, the five vehicles, and the seven, nine, and so forth. When sentient beings receive this treasure of the Dharma, they shall surely attain the fruit.

It is not false. However, among the Buddhas, there is nothing other than the manifestation of the provisional based upon the real; how could there be any real dharma? Therefore, it is merely like a heap of conjured jewels.
Although the Unsurpassed Vehicle is said to be the most ultimate reality, it is entirely the principle inherent within the nature of sentient beings.
Outside the mind, there are no dharmas; hence it is said: "Perfect Bodhi returns to non-attainment. It is like [experiencing something] in a dream.
As for gold and silk, how could there be any actual substance to be obtained? The various paths of the Buddha are established in response to the deluded sentiments of ordinary beings;
when such deluded sentiments do not arise, what "Buddha-path" could there be? That which is called the unconditioned is without arising or ceasing; it is unreal, like flowers in the sky.

Mount Sumeru emerges from the ocean; wind and waves cannot cause it to drift or shake. When the mind is sustained by meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), objects and consciousness cannot distract or delude it.

Yet Mount Sumeru has no substantial reality; it is merely a composite of the four precious substances and the four subtle elements (*paramāṇu*). Meditative concentration likewise has no substantial reality;
it is merely a composite of the various minds, mental factors (*caitta*), and the four divisions [of the aggregates]. Birth and death are like a long night. There is no...
Because they are entangled by ignorance, they sleep both day and night; in Nirvana, which is like the eternal day, wisdom is clear and bright, so they remain awake both day and night.
That one wanders through birth and death is solely due to the six sense faculties; that one finds peace and bliss in Nirvana is likewise solely due to the six sense faculties.

To turn one's back on awakening and unite with the sensory objects is called "inversion," yet in reality there is no decrease [in the nature of the faculties]. To turn one's back on the sensory objects and unite with awakening is called "correct."
In reality, there is no increase; it is merely like the dance of six dragons, which does nothing more than exchange their heads and tails.
Since all phenomena (*dharmas*) are equal, then taking up even a single atom of a phenomenon is itself equal to the ground of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
It is not that apart from all phenomena there exists some other great universal dharma-gate; it is simply that, point by point, [all things are thus].

Every phenomenon is, without exception, a great universal dharma-gate. The path of transformation is bestowed based upon the ground of one true reality, just as trees exist upon the great earth through the four seasons:
sprouting in spring, flourishing in summer, bearing fruit in autumn, and shedding leaves in winter.
They sprout again and again, flourish again and again, bear fruit again and again, and shed leaves again and again; ending and beginning once more, beginning and ending once more, pervading all.
Throughout the ten directions and across the three periods of time, all are the sovereign spiritual powers of the Tathāgata.
